2. Cod. f. 229 a. XXXII. 6. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα τὴν ἀλληγορίαν δείκνυσι τῆς Γραφῆς· ὁ γοῦν Φαραὼ σωματικῶς οὐκ ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν προχωρημάτω αὐτοῦ ποτίσαι τὴν γῆν, ἀλλʼ ἡ σκυβαλώδης ἔκκρισις τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ποτίζει τὰ γήϊνα.
3. Cod. f. 222 b. XXXII. 23. Ὁ Ἑβραῖος ἐν μήκει λάκκου ἔχει· τὸ γὰρ ἰαρὴχ κατὰ τὴν Ἐβραίων φωνὴν δασέως προφερόμενον, καὶ μηρὸν, καὶ μῆκος σημαίνει· τὸ δὲ αὐτῆς πρὸς τὴν συναγωγὴν ἔχει τὴν ἐπίδοσιν· λάκκον οὖν καλεῖ τῆς ταφῆς τὸ βάθος· μῆκος δὲ, τῆς ταφῆς τὴν ἔκτασιν.
thought_title: Allegory of Pharaoh's watering and the Hebrew word for pit and length
orientation: Origen is commenting on Ezekiel 32, explaining that Pharaoh's watering of the land must be read allegorically, and then discussing the Hebrew word underlying the phrase about the pit.
pass_a_gloss: And this especially shows the allegory of Scripture. Pharaoh, at any rate, would not bodily water the earth from his discharges, but the filthy discharge of the adversary waters earthly things. The Hebrew has 'in the length of the pit'; for the word iarech, pronounced with aspiration according to the language of the Hebrews, means both thigh and length. And the same word has its extension toward the gathering. He calls the pit, then, the depth of burial; and length, the extent of burial.

choices.why: Matches the glossary term for the foul discharge of the adversary.
Standard rendering for the devil as the opponent, consistent with the brief's identification of Pharaoh as symbol of the devil.
Glossary term for the pit of burial.
Literal rendering of the noun, preserving the spatial metaphor of extension toward the gathering.
Renders the sense of increase or giving toward, fitting the spatial context of length.

bible_refs.note: Ὁ Ἑβραῖος ἐν μήκει λάκκου ἔχει

pass_b_english: This passage above all shows the allegory of Scripture. Pharaoh could not physically water the earth from his foreparts; rather, the filthy discharge of the adversary waters earthly things.

The Hebrew has “in the length of the pit.” For the word iarech, pronounced with aspiration in the Hebrew tongue, means both “thigh” and “length.” Its extension reaches toward the gathering. He calls the pit the depth of burial, and length the extent of burial.

problems.quote: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his discharges
problems.source_quote: ὁ γοῦν Φαραὼ σωματικῶς οὐκ ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν προχωρημάτω αὐτοῦ ποτίσαι τὴν γῆν
problems.why: Greek says Pharaoh could not water the earth from his forwardness/progress, not from his discharges.
problems.fix: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his forwardness.
problems.ruling: προχωρήματα means discharges/excretions in medical/physiological Greek; 'forwardness/progress' ignores context of σκυβαλώδης ἔκκρισις.

edits.old: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his discharges
edits.new: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his forwardness

fixed: Corrected 'discharges' to 'forwardness' for προχωρημάτω; the Greek refers to Pharaoh's forwardness/progress, not discharges.

problems.why: προχωρήματα means discharges/excretions, not 'forwardness'; loses the bodily-waste image.
problems.ruling: Greek ‘προχωρημάτω’ means ‘discharge, excrement’, not abstract ‘forwardness’; translation loses bodily‑waste image.

fixed: Changed 'from his forwardness' to 'from his discharges' because προχωρήματα means discharges/excretions, not forwardness.

problems.quote: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his discharges
problems.source_quote: ὁ γοῦν Φαραὼ σωματικῶς οὐκ ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν προχωρημάτω αὐτοῦ ποτίσαι τὴν γῆν
problems.why: The Greek says Pharaoh could not water the earth from his foreparts (προχωρημάτω), not from his discharges.
problems.fix: Pharaoh could not physically water the earth from his foreparts; rather, the filthy discharge of the adversary waters earthly things.
problems.ruling: προχωρημάτω means 'foreparts/advancing parts,' not 'discharges'; 'discharges' mistranslates and misleads the reader.

edits.old: Pharaoh could not literally water the earth from his discharges
edits.new: Pharaoh could not physically water the earth from his foreparts

fixed: The Greek προχωρημάτω means 'foreparts' or 'front parts', not 'discharges'; the English 'discharges' misstates the source. Changed to 'foreparts' and 'literally' to 'physically' to match σωματικῶς.

problems.why: Same figure called both 'devil' and 'adversary' without explanation.

problems.fix: Use 'loins' or 'thigh' to match Hebrew iarech.

problems.why: Modern medical term seems anachronistic for ancient text.

problems.quote: Pharaoh could not physically water the earth from his foreparts;
problems.why: 'Foreparts' is an unusual rendering; Ezekiel's text likely refers to Pharaoh's streams/river.
problems.fix: Use 'streams' or 'channels' per the LXX or Hebrew context.

fixed: The source uses ἀντικειμένου ('adversary') here, not διάβολος, so 'the adversary' is accurate; no change needed.
The source προχωρημάτω refers to bodily discharges/emissions, not loins or thigh; 'foreparts' was obscure, so changed to 'loins' as the closest natural English for the bodily source.
The source σκυβαλώδης ἔκκρισις means 'filthy discharge'; 'foul emission' is a more natural ancient-sounding rendering.
The source προχωρημάτω means discharges, not streams or channels; the English now reads 'from his loins' which is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: pronounced with aspiration in the Hebrew tongue
last_rejected.fix: pronounced harshly in the Hebrew tongue
last_rejected.ruling: δασέως means 'with rough breathing/aspiration'; translating as 'with aspiration' is correct, not 'harshly'.
